Hurl
HURL
v.t. (to throw with violence)
From Middle English hurlen, probably imitative or related to Low German hurreln, to toss. The Hebrew word means to cast or throw.

Biblical Definition

The law of the cities of refuge carefully distinguished murder from accidental killing. Among the marks of murder: “But if he thrust him of hatred, or hurl at him by laying of wait, that he die;” then “he that smote him shall surely be put to death; for he is a murderer” (Numbers 35:21). Hatred, ambush and a weapon hurled with intent marked the deed as wilful. By contrast, the man who killed “without enmity” or cast a stone “seeing him not” (35:22-23) could flee to a city of refuge and be safe from the avenger of blood. The law thus looked at the heart behind the hand. God values human life because man is made in His image (Genesis 9:6), and He requires that deliberate murder be punished by the magistrate; yet He also protects the one who kills without malice. Christ deepened the same principle when He taught that hatred itself is murder in the heart (Matthew 5:21-22; 1 John 3:15). The cities of refuge also point to Christ, the refuge to whom guilty sinners flee and in whom they are safe from the avenger.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): HURL, to send or drive with violence; to throw with violence; to utter with vehemence.

expand to see more

HURL, v.t. To send or drive with violence; to throw with violence; as, to hurl a stone or dart.

To utter with vehemence; as, to hurl defiance.

Numbers 35:20 names hurling a missile by laying of wait as a mark of murder.

Hatred and ambush distinguished murder from accidental killing.

The law of the cities of refuge looked at the heart behind the hand.

Key Scripture

Num 35:20 — "But if he thrust him of hatred, or hurl at him by laying of wait, that he die;"

Num 35:21 — "Or in enmity smite him with his hand, that he die: he that smote him shall surely be put to death; for he is a murderer: the revenger of blood shall slay the murderer, when he meeteth him."

Gen 9:6 — "Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man."

Modern Corruption

Modern justice often ignores the moral weight of intent or abandons the biblical principle that wilful murder deserves the magistrate's gravest sentence.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The verb keeps its plain sense.

The principle to recover is the law's careful distinction between malice and accident, and its high view of human life as bearing God's image. Scripture grounds the magistrate's sword in Genesis 9:6 and Romans 13:4, and it judges hatred as murder of the heart. Both civil justice and personal holiness are shaped by it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Middle English hurlen, to throw violently; Numbers 35:20 makes hurling by ambush a mark of murder.

Middle English hurlen, probably imitative.

To throw with violence.

Numbers 35:20 is the only occurrence in the Authorized Version.

Hatred and laying of wait marked the killer as a murderer.

Man's blood is avenged because he bears God's image (Genesis 9:6).
